extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and policymakers interested in education policy, political economy, and moral philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging the proper ends and effects of state-provided education and for morally/economically assessing luxury and consumption. The page argues what education should promote (individuality, practical ability) and how luxury should be defined and evaluated (moral, economic, and justice perspectives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Education's primary purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Education should enable the rising generation to perform intelligently their functions as citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author contrasts classical learning (Greece and Rome) with practical ignorance (e.g., knowledge of national history, political economy, or currency). Curricula should be judged by how much they make competent members of the commonwealth rather than by erudition in ancient literature alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should promote individuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Its aim should be to promote, not to destroy, individuality; human development in its richest diversity (Von Humboldt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education ought to 'aid Nature in perfecting the individual' and give full scope to peculiarities of the young rather than enforcing uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off: state efficiency versus individual development
rubrics_metrics.description: Before deciding the agency for instruction, determine the object of education; the state may be efficient but may not best promote the object if that object is individual development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rigorous, vast state enterprise demands uniform systems which reduce room for individual differences. Efficiency claims must be weighed against loss of individuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid systems that standardize thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The more rigorous the system the less room there will be for the development of individual differences; such systems 'make the mind a mere receptacle' and train people to think alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate schooling models by whether they encourage independent thinking or simply inculcate uniform facts and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of harmful state education
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicators that state education is harmful include contraction of views, deadening of sensibilities, and reduction of minds to repositories of facts and figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples invoked: China (rote learning), Germany (long gymnasium curriculum focused on Latin and Greek), and France — watch for these symptoms as evidence a system is stifling intellectual vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education must train practical ability and independent thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The demand is increasingly 'not what do you know, but what can you do?' — education should produce minds trained to independent thought and practical affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess programs by graduates' readiness for vocation and public life, not merely by their possession of erudite facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid leveling that crushes genius
rubrics_metrics.description: State education's tendency is 'to crush genius and enthrone mediocrity' by leveling all minds to the same standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems that 'stretch' or 'trim' children to fit a uniform standard (Procrustean image) should be judged negatively because they destroy exceptional talents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradualism in educational reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Revolutions in educational systems should be gradual to avoid shocks to the structure of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if state instruction should be limited, the author cautions against sudden abolition of existing institutions because of interwoven interests; policy change should be incremental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect integrity of the individual from state encroachment
rubrics_metrics.description: Jealously guard the integrity of the individual and make the temple of the mind sacred so that neither law nor custom shall enslave it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit the state to its 'true function' in education to avert evils of intellectual and social stagnation observed in other nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of luxury (basic)
rubrics_metrics.description: An object of luxury is everything that does not answer some primary need, and which, costing much money and consequently much labor, is within the reach of only a small number of persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An 'extravagant consumption' destroys the product of many days of labor without bringing any rational satisfaction (example: a lace robe worth ten thousand francs spoiled in a dance). The status of an object as luxury can change over time as production and cost change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extravagance criterion (superfluous + dear)
rubrics_metrics.description: Luxury (extravagance) is that which is both superfluous and dear — it consumes disproportionate labor for no rational satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing J. B. Say and others: mere superfluity that is cheap is less harmful; a thing is properly condemned as luxury when it is both unnecessary and costly in terms of labor expended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify motives behind luxury
rubrics_metrics.description: Three natural and universal feelings give rise to luxury: vanity, sensuality, and the instinct for adornment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding whether luxury springs from vanity (desire to be distinguished), sensuality (pursuit of ever more refined pleasures), or adornment (aesthetic impulse) helps evaluate its moral weight and possible remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanity as ambivalent: stimulant or corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Vanity can be a stimulant for good when public opinion inclines toward virtue, but it can lead to luxury and corruption when public opinion adores riches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social norms can redirect vanity toward virtuous ends (examples: changes in dress norms; John Stuart Mill's proposal that mental occupation reduces love of gewgaws).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensual-rooted luxury escalates and is hard to restrain
rubrics_metrics.description: Luxury rooted in sensuality compels pursuit of ever finer and rarer enjoyments; refinements become niceties and escalate consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (histor and extreme) — Cleopatra swallowing a pearl, Heliogabalus's feasts — illustrate how sensuality drives consumption beyond reason; this motivates dearness and ostentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish ornament/adornment from ostentation (art vs luxury)
rubrics_metrics.description: The instinct for adornment, when cultivated, is aesthetic sentiment that creates art and public monuments; it should not be confounded with ostentation or sensual luxury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art pursues the realization of the beautiful and is 'disinterested'; luxury 'has only one aim — to seem.' Evaluate decorative practices by whether they pursue harmony and beauty accessible to many or serve egotistical display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fashion's moral and economic evils
rubrics_metrics.description: Fashion makes minds frivolous by diverting attention from important matters and causes economic waste by forcing consumption and discarding still-useful goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the impact of changing fashions on social attention and on production costs (designs, models, unsold remnants, price increases), and judge negatively when fashion multiplies waste and raises prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Luxury versus social needs: allocation of labor and capital
rubrics_metrics.description: When many live in destitution, employing large parts of capital and labor to produce superfluities is illegitimate; luxury that diverts labor from producing necessaries is morally wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues (against Baudrillart's tolerant view) that in presence of poverty the production of expensive superfluities (e.g., diamonds) should be condemned because that labor could produce necessities for the poor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual acceptability: luxury as incentive to labor
rubrics_metrics.description: A moderate degree of luxury may be an indispensable stimulant to labor in 'savage' or underdeveloped societies by creating new wants and motivating production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admit limited instrumental luxury where necessary to raise productive effort, but reject it in developed societies where basic needs remain unmet and where luxury no longer justifiably stimulates useful labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical test of consumption reasonableness
rubrics_metrics.description: The line between reasonable consumption and extravagance is whether the satisfaction procured by an object is worth the time and effort necessary to produce it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If obtaining an object diverts human labor from more useful ends, it is wrong. Examples: a cheap Japanese fan is not extravagance if it costs little effort, while a Croesus drinking an expensive wine that consumes twenty days of labor is a bad use of time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold framework for evaluating luxury
rubrics_metrics.description: Luxury should be judged from three points of view: moral (individual development), economical (effect on wealth increase), and justice (compatibility with equitable distribution and remuneration proportionate to useful labor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and moral judgments should consider all three dimensions (the author notes Christianity's condemnation of luxury because it diverts resources from charity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of technological progress in judging luxury
rubrics_metrics.description: Increased productivity from machinery should free human time for cultivation of mind and enjoyment of art and nature, not be channeled into creating more superfluities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether gains in productivity shorten toil and improve leisure for culture, or perversely lengthen toil and intensify consumption of luxury; judge negatively if machinery results in longer hours and more nervous strain while enabling production of superfluities.
